part_title: Lambda Fundamentals and Serverless Application Patterns

scenes.title: More Tools for Building AI Applications
scenes.narration: Welcome to Module Six. So far, we have studied the models and the ways to improve their responses. Now we need to build an application around those models. Imagine a customer asking an online shop to summarise their latest orders. A model cannot safely fetch private order records or decide whether the customer is authorised on its own. We need an API to receive the request, a function to enforce business rules, a data store for order history, and perhaps a queue when processing takes too long for an immediate answer. Keep that customer request in mind as we move through the module. Amazon API Gateway provides the entry point. Lambda runs bounded application logic. Step Functions coordinates work with multiple stages, and messaging services let producers and consumers operate independently. These are not interchangeable building blocks. An API handles how a caller reaches the application; a function runs code; an orchestrator tracks progress; a queue buffers work. Learning which responsibility belongs where is the foundation for the architectures ahead.

scenes.title: AWS Lambda: Serverless Data Processing
scenes.narration: Consider a new file arriving in Amazon S3. We want to validate the file, extract useful metadata and prepare it for an AI search index. Without a serverless design, we might run a server continuously and periodically check for new files. With Lambda, the arrival of an object can trigger a function instead. Follow that sequence: the event identifies the bucket and object key; Lambda starts an execution environment and invokes the handler; the handler reads the authorised object, performs its transformation, and writes or forwards the result. The function doesn't need to own a permanently running web server. But notice the boundary between a small transformation and a large processing job. If the file takes hours to process, a single Lambda execution is not the right unit of work. We could start a dedicated processing service or a Step Functions workflow and store the job state separately. The useful design decision here is to match Lambda to short, event-driven processing rather than calling it an all-purpose compute replacement.

scenes.title: What Is AWS Lambda?
scenes.narration: Let's look inside a Lambda function configuration. The handler is the entry point that receives an event and context; it is not the same as the event source. The runtime provides the language execution environment, and the deployment package or container image contains our application code and dependencies. The execution role controls which AWS APIs the code can call. For instance, a function that reads source documents from S3 does not automatically receive permission to invoke Bedrock or write to DynamoDB. Those permissions must be granted deliberately. Memory, timeout and concurrency settings control how the function runs and scales. Now compare two ways the function may be called. An API request can require a synchronous response, while an event-driven invocation may be retried without the original caller waiting. That distinction changes error handling. If a message is delivered twice, the handler must avoid duplicating a payment or starting the same costly inference twice. Remember the separation: event source invokes, runtime executes, role authorises, and the handler performs the task.

scenes.title: Example: Serverless Website
scenes.narration: Imagine opening a simple shopping website. The browser first downloads HTML, styles and JavaScript, commonly from static hosting and a content delivery layer. When the customer asks for a live order summary, the browser calls an HTTPS API rather than downloading a new static page. API Gateway matches the request to a route and forwards it to Lambda. The function checks the caller's identity and requested order, reads authorised data from the backend and returns a structured response. The browser then displays the result. Notice that the static website and the dynamic API serve different purposes: the static files can be cached broadly, while private order data must be retrieved through controlled backend operations. To extend the example with generative AI, Lambda can obtain just the relevant records and call Bedrock to produce a readable summary. The model does not receive unrestricted database access. Also distinguish an API authorization check from a Lambda IAM role: the former controls who may request the action, while the latter controls what the function can do in AWS.

scenes.title: Example: Order History Application
scenes.narration: Now follow an order through its lifecycle. A customer places an order, the application records its details, and the order history must become available for later lookup. A request to view the history should retrieve records for the authenticated customer, not scan every customer's data. A Lambda handler can implement that lookup and format the result for the client. But the system may also need to send a confirmation, update an audit record and enrich the data for search. These side effects should not all block the customer's original response. Separate the fast read path from background processing triggered by new orders. Each worker should have a clear responsibility and a reliable way to retry failures. If the same order-created event arrives twice, use an order identifier to prevent duplicate side effects. For the AI assistant, retrieve the specific authorised records first, then ask Bedrock to explain them in natural language. This example shows the progression from an event or API call, through Lambda business logic, to a trustworthy customer-facing result.
